concept.name: Continuous auction
concept.definition: A trading mechanism in which orders are matched whenever they arrive during the trading session: an incoming order executes immediately against compatible resting orders in the order book, so trading proceeds continuously rather than at discrete crossing times.
concept.intuition: The market never waits — the moment your order can match something in the book, it trades.
concept.mechanics: The matching engine applies price-time (or venue-specific) priority continuously: marketable orders sweep resting liquidity, unexecuted limit orders join the book, and each execution updates the last traded price that others reference.
concept.failure_modes: Continuous matching can amplify speed advantages and fragility: in fast markets, resting liquidity is pulled faster than it can be replaced, producing cascade moves and flash events that a batch auction would have dampened.
concept.misconceptions: Continuous trading does not mean continuous liquidity — the book can be empty at any instant, and the 'current price' is just the last match, which may be stale or a small odd lot.
concept.example: From 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET, Nasdaq's continuous book matches incoming equity orders immediately against resting orders, between the Opening Cross and the Closing Cross.
